H1.text: A maize root tip makes more than seventeen thousand five hundred new cells every hour.

H2.text: A watermelon cell can grow up to three lakh fifty thousand times bigger. And a mango tree keeps growing all its life.

H3.text: Aarav wanted numbers. He measured a bean seedling with a ruler every day. He asked: how do we measure growth? And does a plant grow by the same amount each day?

H4.text: Here is the short answer. We measure growth as length, area, weight or cell number. And the pattern can be steady, or it can keep doubling.

H5.text: By the end, you will know the phases of growth, arithmetic and geometric growth, growth rates, and what growth needs.

B2.text: Growth is a permanent increase in size. It cannot be reversed. A balloon that fills with air and goes flat again is not growing.

B3.text: Plants grow all their life. This is called indeterminate growth. It happens because plants have meristems, groups of cells that keep dividing.

B4.text: Growth can be measured as fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume or cell number. A pollen tube is measured by its length. A leaf, by its surface area.

Z1.text: Let's zoom into a growing root.

Z2.text: A seedling root gets longer only near its tip.

Z3.text: Zoom to the tip. Behind the root cap lie three zones, one after another: meristematic, elongation and maturation.

Z4.text: Zoom to the cells. Meristematic cells divide, with dense cytoplasm, big nuclei and thin walls. Elongating cells get bigger, with a large vacuole. Maturing cells reach full size and thicken their walls.

L1.text: Now, how fast does growth happen? There are two patterns.

L2.text: In arithmetic growth, after a cell divides, only one daughter cell keeps dividing. The other one grows up and matures.

L3.text: So the root gets longer by the same amount each time. Plot length against time and you get a straight line. Length at time t equals starting length plus r times t.

L4.text: In geometric growth, both daughter cells keep dividing. One cell becomes two, then four, then eight.

L5.text: At first, growth is slow. This is the lag phase. Then it shoots up fast. This is the log, or exponential, phase.

L6.text: But nutrients run short, so growth slows down and stops. This is the stationary phase. The whole curve looks like the letter S, so it is called a sigmoid curve.

L7.text: Here, final size equals starting size times e to the power r t. The r is the relative growth rate. It shows how well a plant makes new material, so it is also called the efficiency index.

C1.text: We can compare growth in two ways.

C2.text: Absolute growth rate is the total growth per unit time.

C3.text: Relative growth rate is the growth per unit time compared with the starting size. Small things can have a big relative rate.

D1.text: What does a plant need to grow?

D2.text: Water. Water makes cells swell and press on their walls. This pressure, called turgor, helps cells stretch. Water is also where the enzymes do their work.

D3.text: Oxygen, to release energy from food. And nutrients, to build new protoplasm and to give energy.

D4.text: Each plant also needs a temperature range that suits it best, called its optimum range. Signals like light and gravity also guide some stages of growth.

D5.text: Your turn. In a root, one daughter cell keeps dividing while the other matures. Is that arithmetic or geometric growth? Pause and decide.

D6.text: Arithmetic! Only one cell keeps dividing, so the root adds the same length each time, a straight line.

T1.text: Remember this. Arithmetic is a straight line. Geometric is an S.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Two leaves, A and B.

W2.text: Leaf A starts at five square centimetres. Leaf B starts at fifty. In the same time, each one grows by five square centimetres.

W3.text: So their absolute growth is the same, five square centimetres each.

W4.text: But leaf A grew five out of five, that is one hundred percent. Leaf B grew five out of fifty, only ten percent. Leaf A has the higher relative growth rate.

X2.text: Many students think geometric growth keeps rising forever.

X3.text: But nutrients become limited. Growth slows and the curve flattens into the stationary phase. That is why it is an S, not a straight rocket.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As statement questions on the phases of growth, the two growth equations and the sigmoid curve.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Read the four statements. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is D. Statements two, three and four are correct.

A2.text: L t equals L zero plus r t describes arithmetic growth. In the geometric equation, r is the relative growth rate, the efficiency index.

A3.text: The sigmoid curve has lag, log and stationary phases. But in arithmetic growth only one daughter cell keeps dividing, so statement one is wrong.
